name: Narrative / Adventure
description: Story first: branching choices, characters and a world to explore and interact with.

pillars.name: Characters You Care About
pillars.feeling: I want to know what happens to them
pillars.rulesOut: cast members who exist only to deliver exposition

pillars.name: Choices That Matter
pillars.feeling: the story is shaped by what I did
pillars.rulesOut: branches that collapse straight back together

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A story-driven adventure where the player's choices decide who survives a long night in a small town.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Explore a scene.
2. Talk to characters and examine clues.
3. Make a choice.
4. See its consequences in the next scene.

docs.title: Story
docs.summary: The narrative and how the player's choices shape it.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can follow a story that changes with my choices.
- As a player, I can replay to see other outcomes.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A chapter summary after each chapter.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Every chapter ends with a major choice.

docs.title: Choices and Consequences
docs.summary: Which choices matter, and how and when they pay off.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can make choices that matter later.
- As a player, I can see a hint that a choice was remembered.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A small notification when a choice will have consequences.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Consequences show up within two chapters.

docs.title: Story State
docs.summary: Story flags, branching logic, and keeping saves valid as the story changes.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Story flags are gameplay tags stored in a story subsystem. Dialogue, quests and scenes check flags to decide what happens.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `UStorySubsystem`: story flags and chapter state

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Story flags saved with the game.

docs.title: Script
docs.summary: The written story: scenes, branches and dialogue lines.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chapter scripts | Data | Placeholder | To source |
| Branch outlines | Data | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Grounded, small-town dialogue; characters speak in their own voices.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text: - Writers familiar with branching narrative tools.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Exposition dumps.

docs.title: Dialogue
docs.summary: Conversations: how they're presented and chosen from.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can talk to characters and choose what to say.
- As a player, I can see who's speaking.
- As a player, I can review what was said.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Subtitles with the speaker's name.
- Choices that hint at their tone.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Important choices can't be skipped.
- Dialogue can be advanced but never auto-skips choices.

docs.title: Dialogue System
docs.summary: How dialogue is authored, triggered and displayed.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Dialogue is authored as graphs; nodes are lines and choices, with conditions on story flags.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UDialogueGraph`: an authored conversation
- `UDialogueComponent`: plays a dialogue on an actor

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Dialogue graphs as assets.
- Localization strings per line.

docs.title: Voice Over
docs.summary: Recorded lines, by character and scene.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recorded lines per character | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Natural, understated performances.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Voice actors with experience in games.
- Recording at a consistent quality.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Overacted performances.

docs.title: Exploration
docs.summary: Moving through scenes and examining or using things in them.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can walk through scenes and examine objects.
- As a player, I can find clues that open new options.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Interactable objects highlight when I look at them.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Nothing important is hidden behind pixel hunting.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The player traces for interactables; the closest one shows a prompt, and interacting runs its action.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UInteractionComponent`: finds interactables and shows prompts
- `IInteractable`: interface for anything that can be used

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Interaction ranges and prompts per object.

docs.title: Characters
docs.summary: The cast: who they are, how they change, and how the player meets them.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can meet a cast with distinct personalities.
- As a player, I can see characters change through the story.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Character portraits in dialogue.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Every main character has an arc.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can watch short scenes at key moments.
- As a player, I can skip scenes I've already seen.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Letterboxing during cutscenes.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Cutscenes are under two minutes.

docs.title: Sequencer Setup
docs.summary: How cinematics are built and triggered with Sequencer.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Cinematics are Level Sequences triggered by story events; the player camera blends into the sequence and back.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `UCinematicSubsystem`: plays sequences and handles skipping

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - One Level Sequence per cutscene.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.
